topic.topic: How Gift Cards Make Money for Retailers

learningValue: Tests whether the filing-backed forecast angle earns viewed-vs-swiped and shares on the same facts as the long-form.
selectedTitle: Who Keeps the Money on Unused Gift Cards?
hookCandidates: In the US, Starbucks cards don't expire. Yet by our math, Starbucks booked $222.4 million of card money as sales in fiscal 2025, with no drink served.
Look at the gift card in your drawer. The company that sold it has already estimated how likely you are to spend it.
Who keeps the money on an unspent gift card?
A gift card is money the store owes you. Some of that debt slowly turns into the store's sales.
Starbucks booked $222.4 million in its latest fiscal year from card money it doesn't expect to see redeemed.

beats.text: In the US, Starbucks cards don't expire. Yet by our math, Starbucks booked $222.4 million of card money as sales in fiscal 2025, with no drink served.
The reason is a forecast. From its own history, Starbucks estimates how much will never be redeemed, and calls that share breakage.
None of this touches your balance. Each time a card gets spent, a predicted slice moves into sales.
Part can also go to the government under unclaimed property laws.
So who keeps the money? The store keeps the money it predicted you'd never spend, but only if you never do. Your balance is still yours. Spend it, and prove the forecast wrong.

storyPlan.thesis: Unspent gift card money is not grabbed when a card goes quiet: companies predict from their own history how much will never be spent and book that share as sales, a little at a time.

conflict.wants: The store wants revenue it can count on; the holder wants their balance.
conflict.obstacle: Cards that never expire can't simply be taken back.
conflict.stakes: Starbucks booked $222.4 million this way in one year.

storyPlan.misconception: The store takes the money when a card expires.
storyPlan.originalAngle: The company's own filing explains the forecast in one line; many explainers stop at 'stores profit from forgotten cards'.

problems.quote: The store keeps the money it predicted you'd never spend. The rest is still yours.
problems.fix: Implies part of the balance is no longer the holder's. It is: the card has no expiry and no balance-reducing fees. The store keeps it only if the holder never spends it. (Found in the final editorial read, after the automated checks passed.)

problems.quote: The store keeps the share it predicted you'd never spend.
problems.fix: Answer the question in its own words: 'the store keeps the money it predicted you'd never spend', then end on what the viewer can do.

problems.quote: Starbucks estimates how much money will never be redeemed.
problems.fix: Name the thing: the company calls that share breakage. One plain word the viewer can repeat.

problems.quote: It doesn't take that money from anyone.
problems.fix: Keep; it corrects the misconception directly. Tighten the second sentence so the timing is clear: a slice moves into sales each time someone else uses a card.

keep: The contradiction hook with the filing number
The unclaimed property caveat, stated as the filing states it

changes: b2: named the share (breakage) in a tighter sentence
b3: states exactly what the filing supports (no fees reduce balances; breakage moves with redemptions) instead of a broad 'nothing is taken'
b4: tightened the caveat to the filing's own claim
b5: the payoff answers the question in its own words and ends on the viewer's move
overall: trimmed from 118 to about 107 words for a 35-45 second read
b5: factual correction: breakage is a forecast, not a transfer; the whole balance stays spendable
